intro: This guide takes your group through Confessions (For Teens) in thirteen weeks, one chapter each week. It’s written for teenagers aged about 13 to 18 and works well for a youth group, a homeschool or a small group. Augustine’s Confessions is the life story of a brilliant, restless young man, told as a prayer to God: his teenage rebellion, his years chasing success and clever answers, his mother’s prayers, his conversion in a garden in Milan, and his discovery that “our heart is restless, until it repose in Thee.” Teens will find a surprising amount of their own world in it.

Each session takes about 30 to 40 minutes. Welcome everyone and say the memory verse together. Read the chapter, either aloud together or at home beforehand. Talk it through using the chapter’s three questions, which come with answers to help you. Do the activity, which takes about 10 minutes. Then close by praying the chapter’s prayer, or one of your own.

To prepare, read the chapter yourself and look over the activity so you know what you’ll need; most weeks need nothing more than paper and pens. Augustine is honest about sex, peer pressure, a long relationship outside marriage, grief and the death of a close friend, and in Chapter 5 he describes not wanting to live after a loss. Read those chapters ahead, keep the talk respectful, and never ask anyone to share their own sins or struggles with the group: personal reflection stays private. Be ready to follow up quietly with anyone who seems to be carrying grief or dark thoughts, and know where to point them for help, including a crisis line where you live.

weeks.summary: Augustine opens his life story with a prayer, not a birth date: God made us for himself, and our hearts are restless until they rest in him. He looks back honestly at his childhood in North Africa, from a jealous baby to a boy who prayed not to be beaten at school, wept over stories, lied and cheated at games, yet still had real gifts from God. The big idea: the restlessness we feel is a homing signal, because we were made for God and nothing smaller will satisfy us.

memory_verse.text: As a deer pants for flowing streams, so pants my soul for you, O God.

activity.title: What Am I Hungry For?
steps: Give everyone a sheet of paper and ask them to list, for themselves, five things people their age reach for to fill a quiet or empty moment.
As a group, call out some of the items without saying whose list they came from, and write them up where everyone can see.
Discuss: which of these are good gifts in themselves, and which promise more than they can give?
Read Augustine’s line, “our heart is restless, until it repose in Thee,” and ask what it would look like to bring that restlessness to God instead.
Invite everyone to write Augustine’s first line in their own words at the bottom of their sheet and keep it.

weeks.summary: At sixteen, with a year off school, Augustine gives in to desire, shrugs off his mother’s warnings, and even invents sins to impress his friends. One night he and some friends steal pears they don’t want and throw them to the pigs, and he admits he did it simply because it was forbidden, and would never have done it alone. The big idea: sin loves an audience and can want wrong things just because they are wrong, but God can melt even that.

memory_verse.text: The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately sick; who can understand it?

activity.title: Would I Do This Alone?
steps: Read out four or five everyday group situations, such as a joke at someone’s expense, a screenshot being passed round, or a dare at a sleepover.
For each one, have the group stand on one side of the room for “easy to say no to” and the other for “hard to say no to.”
Ask a few volunteers why the group makes these things harder or easier, without anyone sharing a real story.
Together, come up with three short, natural ways to say “I’m out” that don’t lecture anyone.
Challenge everyone to ask themselves this week, when a group says “Let’s go,” whether they would do it alone.

weeks.summary: At seventeen Augustine arrives in Carthage, in love with the idea of love, hooked on sad plays, and proud of being top of his class. Reading Cicero’s Hortensius sets him on fire to love wisdom, but when he opens the Bible he looks down on its plain style, and joins the Manichees, who promise clever answers and say sin isn’t really you. The big idea: pride can make us skip the truth that asks us to bow, and Jesus says the kingdom belongs to those willing to be taught like children.

memory_verse.text: Truly, I say to you, unless you turn and become like children, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven.

activity.title: Reading as a Learner
steps: Have everyone open to Mark 1 and read it quietly to themselves.
Ask each person to write down one thing they understand and one thing they don’t.
Gather a few of the “don’t understand” points and talk them through together, without rushing to have every answer.
Discuss: what is the difference between reading the Bible as a critic and reading it as “a little one”?
Encourage everyone to keep reading Mark this week in the same way.

weeks.summary: Monica grieves over her son’s new religion and dreams that one day he will stand where she stands. A bishop tells her to let him read and to pray, and sends her away with the words, “it is not possible that the son of these tears should perish.” Meanwhile Augustine sells the skill of winning arguments and lives with a woman he has not married, and they have a son, Adeodatus. The big idea: prayers can take years without being lost, and sometimes prayer does more than another argument.

memory_verse.text: Those who sow in tears shall reap with shouts of joy!

activity.title: A Week of Quiet Prayer
steps: Give everyone a small card.
Ask them to write, for themselves, the first name of one person they would like to see come to know God, perhaps someone they have quietly given up on.
Talk together about the bishop’s advice to Monica: why might praying and letting someone read do more than winning an argument?
Spend a minute in silence while everyone prays for the person on their card.
Encourage them to keep the card somewhere they will see it and pray for that person every day this week, or to thank someone who has prayed for them.

weeks.summary: Augustine’s closest childhood friend falls ill, is baptised while unconscious, and then dies after rejecting Augustine’s mocking joke about it. Augustine describes his grief with painful honesty: everything looked like death, he wanted neither to live nor to die, and in time friends helped him heal. Looking back, he sees he had loved his friend as if he would never die, and concludes that we should love our friends in God. The big idea: friends are a great gift, but they are not meant to be our god; love held in God is never finally lost.

memory_verse.text: The LORD is near to the brokenhearted and saves the crushed in spirit.

activity.title: What Good Friends Do
steps: Read aloud Augustine’s list of what he loved in his friends: talking and joking together, doing kind things for one another, reading together, being silly or serious together.
In small groups, have teens add three more things that make a friendship good.
Discuss: what is the difference between loving a friend and making a friend your whole world?
Ask everyone to think privately of someone who has lost a person they love this year.
Invite them to send that person a short message this week simply saying they remember.

weeks.summary: Faustus, the great Manichee teacher, turns out to know little, and Augustine’s trust in the movement breaks. He decides to move to Rome, lies to his mother at the harbour and sails while she prays all night that he won’t go. In Rome he nearly dies of a fever, admits the Manichees appealed to his pride by letting him say “it wasn’t really me,” and then wins a post in Milan. The big idea: God’s “no” is not the same as God not caring, and healing starts when we own what we did.

memory_verse.text: The heart of man plans his way, but the LORD establishes his steps.

activity.title: Plans and Steps
steps: Ask everyone to draw a simple road map of how they once expected something to go, such as a year at school, a friendship or a team season, and how it actually went.
Invite a few volunteers to describe a detour that turned out well, keeping it light.
Read Proverbs 16:9 and talk about how Monica’s unanswered prayer that night became part of the answer to her lifelong prayer.
Discuss why “it wasn’t really me” is such a tempting excuse, and what changes when we say “that was me.”
Ask everyone to think privately of one thing they need to own this week, and to say “that was me, and I’m sorry” to God or to the person involved.

weeks.summary: In Milan, Ambrose welcomes Augustine like a father, and Augustine goes to hear him preach only to judge his style, but slowly finds that what Ambrose says is true. He discovers that the Christianity he had mocked for years was a cartoon, leaves the Manichees and becomes a learner, realising how much of life everyone already takes on trust. Monica arrives, calm and sure she will see him believe. The big idea: kindness and steady listening can move someone toward God, and what people reject is often a caricature of the faith.

memory_verse.text: So faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ.

activity.title: Cartoon or the Real Thing?
steps: Ask the group to list, without names, common things people say Christians believe or are like.
Sort them into two columns: “what the church actually teaches” and “a cartoon of it.”
Discuss how Augustine spent years attacking a cartoon, and how he found out the truth.
Ask: who has been an Ambrose to you, someone whose kindness made you keep listening?
Encourage everyone to pick one hard question about Christianity and look for a careful answer this week, from a pastor or a fair explanation.

weeks.summary: On his way to give a speech full of flattering lies, Augustine passes a carefree drunk beggar and realises his ambition is making him more anxious than the beggar. His friend Alypius, dragged to the gladiator fights, vows to keep his eyes shut, but one roar from the crowd makes him look, and he is hooked and becomes “one of the throng.” God later frees Alypius, who grows into a man of real integrity. The big idea: what you keep looking at, you start to become, so lean on God rather than on your own strength.

memory_verse.text: Do not be deceived: “Bad company ruins good morals.”

activity.title: One of the Throng
steps: Read aloud the moment Alypius opens his eyes in the arena.
Discuss: what are today’s versions of the arena, the things people say they can watch without being affected?
Ask why Augustine says Alypius was “bold rather than resolute,” and what real strength looks like instead.
Have everyone write down privately one thing they watch or scroll that leaves them feeling like “one of the throng.”
Challenge them to skip it completely this week, and to practise a simple line like “I’m not watching that.”

weeks.summary: Augustine plans a career marriage, and the woman he has lived with for about fifteen years, the mother of his son, is sent back to Africa; she vows to stay faithful to God while he cannot even wait for his wedding. At the same time his mind clears: he learns that evil is not a thing but a good will twisted away from God. But the philosophers’ books lacked the one thing that mattered: the Word made flesh, and the humility to come to him. The big idea: knowing about God is not the same as coming to him, and only the humble Christ can reach the wrongs in our lives.

memory_verse.text: And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory, glory as of the only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth.

activity.title: Head and Heart
steps: Draw two columns on a board: “What Augustine was learning about God” and “How Augustine was treating people.”
Fill them in together from the chapter.
Discuss: how can someone’s ideas about God improve while their life still hurts people?
Talk about what changes when God comes close in Jesus, humble enough to touch real lives.
Ask everyone to think privately of someone they have treated as unimportant, and to consider one honest apology this week with no excuses attached.

weeks.summary: Augustine’s doubts are mostly gone, but his will is chained by habit. He hears how the famous professor Victorinus finally confessed Christ in public, and how two officials gave up their careers after reading about Antony, and he is ashamed of his old prayer, “Give me chastity and continency, only not yet.” He explains how a wrong desire becomes a habit and a habit becomes a necessity. The big idea: “not yet” has no end date, and habits grow stronger the longer we wait.

memory_verse.text: For I do not do the good I want, but the evil I do not want is what I keep on doing.

activity.title: The Chain of Habit
steps: Read aloud Augustine’s description: a wrong want becomes a habit, and a habit becomes a necessity.
Draw the chain on a board with three links and ask the group for everyday, non-personal examples of how each link forms, such as screen time or snacking at midnight.
Discuss: why does “in a minute” or “not yet” feel so harmless?
Ask everyone to write down for themselves, privately, one “not yet” in their own life and one concrete step they could take against it today.
Encourage them to tell one trusted person what they are doing.

weeks.summary: In a small garden in Milan, Augustine wrestles with a divided will, hears his old habits whispering, and weeps under a fig tree crying, “Why not now?” A child’s voice chants, “Take up and read,” and he opens Paul’s letters to Romans 13:13–14, and the darkness of doubt lifts. Alypius joins him, and Monica rejoices to see her prayers answered. The big idea: the moment of surrender comes when we stop saying “tomorrow” and say “why not now?”

memory_verse.text: But put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh, to gratify its desires.

activity.title: Make No Provision
steps: Read Romans 13:8–14 aloud together, slowly.
Discuss why the garden moment was the end of a long road, not a random Bible lucky dip.
Ask: what does it mean in everyday life to “make no provision for the flesh”? List practical examples together, such as moving a phone out of the bedroom.
Have everyone write down privately one thing they could remove that makes their own “not yet” easy.
Close by reading Augustine’s question together: “Why not now?”

weeks.summary: Augustine resigns quietly and is baptised by Ambrose with Alypius and his son Adeodatus, who later dies young. Waiting at Ostia, he and Monica share a moment at a window when their talk of heaven seems to touch God himself; days later she falls ill and dies, saying, “Nothing is far to God.” Augustine holds back his tears through the funeral, then finally weeps, and asks readers not to mock but to pray. The big idea: faith does not switch off grief; we can believe someone is with God and still weep that they are not with us.

memory_verse.text: But we do not want you to be uninformed, brothers, about those who are asleep, that you may not grieve as others do who have no hope.

activity.title: Say It in Words
steps: Read aloud Monica’s words at the window and her last request.
Discuss: why did Augustine think he shouldn’t cry, and why does he later say he was wrong?
Talk about the difference between grieving without hope and grieving with hope.
Give everyone a few minutes to write a short note, for themselves to send or keep, telling someone who loves them what they mean to them.
Encourage them to say it or send it this week, in real words.

weeks.summary: In the last books of the Confessions, Augustine tells what he is now: a bishop still tempted by pleasure, curiosity and love of praise. He marvels at the vast palace of memory, prays his famous “Too late loved I Thee,” asks what time is, and reads Genesis to find that “my weight is my love,” carrying us wherever we go. The book ends looking forward to God’s eternal Sabbath rest. The big idea: your heart will love something and be carried by it, and only in God does the restless heart find rest.

memory_verse.text: So then, there remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God.

activity.title: Where Is My Love Carrying Me?
steps: Read aloud Augustine’s line, “My weight, is my love; thereby am I borne, whithersoever I am borne.”
Discuss what he means: how do the things we love pull us in a direction?
Give everyone five quiet minutes to write, for themselves, an honest answer to: what do I love most, and where is it carrying me?
Read the “Too late loved I Thee” prayer aloud together.
Invite each person to write one sentence of their own prayer asking, seeking and knocking, and to keep it.
